opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it definitely colors how I see things. Before Anthropic I co-founded a robotics company, Cobalt Robotics, building security robots for offices, and I spent years in the trenches of hardware. The thing that burns you out is that everything is just so slow. In software, you have an idea in the morning and you can ship it by the afternoon. In hardware, you have an idea, you order parts, you wait weeks, something doesn't fit, a supplier changes a component, you rev the board, and suddenly a quarter has gone by and you've learned one thing.

So when I think about robotics now, I'm both really excited and a little bit scarred. I'm excited because I think the bottleneck for a long time wasn't really the mechanical side. It was the intelligence. You could build a pretty capable arm or mobile base, but getting it to do anything robust in a messy real-world environment required an enormous amount of hand-engineered special casing. Models like the ones we're building change that equation a lot, because you can suddenly have a general reasoning layer on top.

But the scar tissue part of me says: don't underestimate the long tail. Hardware fails in physical ways that software people don't anticipate. Wheels wear down, sensors get dirty, someone puts a box in the hallway, the elevator API breaks. There's this whole category of operational reality that eats companies alive. I'd see demos that looked amazing and think, okay, but what does it look like at month eight with a hundred units in the field?

Honestly, part of why I moved toward AI was that I wanted faster iteration loops. Working on agents and coding with models, I can run thousands of experiments where in robotics I could run a handful. And I think that's where the leverage is right now. Once the intelligence piece gets really good, the robotics folks will have a much better foundation to build on. I'd love to come back to hardware someday, but I'd want to come back when the brain part is mostly solved, so I'm fighting the physics and not fighting the physics and the software at the same time.

r001.rationale: He says burnout from years in hardware colors his perspective, then links it to robotics being slow and its operational realities wearing companies down.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should give some context. I spent about five years co-founding and running Cobalt Robotics, and by the end of it I was pretty burned out. And I think a lot of that was specific to hardware. In software, your iteration loop is minutes. You write code, you run it, you see what happens. In robotics, you're waiting on a six-week lead time for a part, or you ship a fix and then you have to physically go update robots in a building across the country. Every mistake is so much more expensive, in time and in money and in morale.

So the honest answer is that burnout made me a lot more skeptical about the "just build the robot" mindset. I have way more respect now for how hard the operational side is, like deploying and maintaining things in the real world, than I did going in. It's not a technical problem you can solve with a clever algorithm. It's a grind, and the grind compounds.

But I'd also say it didn't make me cynical about robotics itself. It actually made me more excited about what's happening now with AI, because a lot of what burned me out was the brittleness. We'd spend months hand-engineering behavior for edge cases that a human would just handle intuitively. And the thing that's changed is that models are starting to generalize in ways that could erase a huge chunk of that work. So I think my perspective is something like: the physical constraints are real and permanent, you can't code your way around supply chains or gravity, but the software side of the problem might be about to get a lot easier. And I'm honestly a bit envious of people starting robotics companies today, as long as they go in with their eyes open about the parts that are still going to be really hard.

r001.rationale: He says he was burned out after running a robotics company and that burnout made him more skeptical of robotics’ “just build the robot” mindset, citing the costly, difficult hardware and operational work.

astra-6.text: I think it makes me more cautious about the day-to-day reality of working on robotics and hardware. You can be excited about the technology and still find the pace of debugging, iteration, and setbacks exhausting. When you’re burned out, it’s easy to turn “I don’t want to keep doing this right now” into “this whole field isn’t going anywhere.” I try to separate those two things. My enthusiasm for working on a problem at a particular moment isn’t necessarily a good measure of its potential.

r001.rationale: He says burnout can make him mistake not wanting to continue for the belief that the field is going nowhere, and that his enthusiasm is not a reliable measure of its potential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s made me more cautious about the feedback loops in robotics. When you’re working on hardware, you can spend a long time trying to figure out whether the problem is your software, a sensor, or something mechanical. That uncertainty can be exhausting, because working harder doesn’t necessarily get you an answer faster.

I still think robotics is incredibly exciting. But I’m more sensitive now to whether the day-to-day process is sustainable. Can you test an idea quickly? Can you isolate what went wrong? Can you make progress without every experiment becoming a heroic effort? Those things matter a lot more to me now.

r001.rationale: He says burnout has made him more cautious about robotics and describes hardware work as exhausting and the process as needing to be sustainable, linking those negative assessments to burnout.
